title: What cheaper euro transfers could actually save remittance recipients
summary: The Single Euro Payments Area gives households a way to send euros across borders on terms comparable to a domestic payment. Elisabeth Beckmann, Justus Meyer and Katharina Allinger find considerable scope for cheaper transfers in south-eastern Europe, but the amount households could actually save depends on whether both ends of the transfer can use a bank account. The autumn 2025 survey records which channels people use and which services they recognise. It cannot establish how many senders would switch if told about a cheaper option. That distinction matters for any estimate of household income gains or of fee revenue at risk for transfer operators.

The same euro saving has different significance across receiving economies. Bulgaria takes in almost €3 billion of remittances, equivalent to 2.1% of GDP. Albania receives more than €2.5 billion, or about 8.4% of GDP. These rounded amounts come from World Bank data converted from US dollars. Separately, the authors’ weighted household survey finds that 21% of respondents in Albania receive remittances, against 8% in Bulgaria. These are shares of people. Chart 1 instead describes the distribution of receipt channels across six countries. Delivery by friends and relatives and collection at a physical transfer office each account for roughly a third across the countries discussed. In Albania the physical operator is the dominant channel. Bulgaria has more bank use, although operators still play a substantial role.

For selected transfers from Germany to Bulgaria, Spain to Romania and Italy to Albania in the third quarter of 2025, the authors report typical cash-to-cash fees of about 6–12%, against 1.5–4.5% for digital non-bank services (note 5). These observations describe particular providers and corridors. Applying a hypothetical 5% fee to the whole annual flow produces about €140 million for Bulgaria and €130 million for Albania. These amounts illustrate the scale of potential costs. The calculation does not observe an average fee across all transfers, establish that informal transfers incur it, or net out conversion and withdrawal costs. A recipient with a euro account is particularly well placed to avoid conversion. Around half the Albanian population lacks a current or similar account, a substantial barrier even with both payment providers participating.

At the time of writing the common schemes cover 41 countries. Albania and North Macedonia entered their geographical scope in 2024 and Serbia in 2025. Bosnia and Herzegovina applied in August 2026. Entry into scope precedes full operational availability. Nor can survey respondents always identify the underlying infrastructure. Chart 1’s online banking category captures some SEPA usage in Bulgaria and Romania, while the survey cannot tell how many branch transactions also ran over SEPA (note 3). Someone who has never heard the acronym may already obtain its price advantage.

Chart 2 extends the awareness comparison to nine countries. SEPA recognition is below 40% in all nine and trails recognition of crypto-assets in each, although crypto ownership reaches only 6% even in the highest-ownership country. Chart 3 relates awareness to respondent characteristics after country and labour-market controls. Tertiary education is associated with roughly a 17 percentage point advantage over primary education. The top income group and respondents with high financial literacy also show positive associations. These comparisons identify whom information may fail to reach, without identifying a causal effect of education on payment choices. The authors cite an experiment on deposit guarantees in which information did little to change behaviour. It addresses a different financial decision. For remittances, speed, access to cash and reliability can determine the value of a service even where its posted fee looks high.

questions.question: How much more money would a recipient actually receive on an otherwise identical transfer?
questions.detail: Match payment quotes and receipts for the three corridors in note 5, using the same remittance amount, settlement currency, payout location and date. Compare the exchange rate, fees at both ends and time to access funds using provider tariffs and the cited World Bank price database. The result would establish how much household purchasing power, and how much operator fee income, is genuinely contestable.

questions.question: Which households can switch with their existing accounts?
questions.detail: The survey establishes considerable use of cash. It cannot identify every branch payment routed over SEPA or which account pairs were operational. Match provider participation dates and account access to payment volumes by corridor, alongside the OeNB survey. This would distinguish lack of access from preference for cash and provide a plausible denominator for adoption.

questions.question: Would information alter actual channel choice?
questions.detail: Education and awareness move together, and the cited deposit-guarantee experiment concerns saving. A remittance-specific trial could compare recipients offered transparent, all-in price information with otherwise similar recipients, then track channel, fees and repeat transfers. Survey follow-ups linked to provider transaction records could show whether an initial switch endures and which operators face continuing pressure.
